title: Die Goldkinder
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 1, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 85. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 85, which opens like the fisherman’s tale and then becomes something else. A poor fisherman lands a golden fish that buys its life with a castle, on the one condition that he never say where the fortune came from; twice his wife wheedles the secret out of him and twice the castle is gone in an instant. The third time the fish has itself cut into six pieces, and out of them come two golden children, two golden foals and two golden lilies that show, by standing fresh or wilting or falling, how the brothers fare in the world. One is shamed by mockery and turns home; the other hides his gold under a bearskin, wins a bride, and is turned to stone until his twin comes for him. Spelling follows the 1857 edition (daß, gieng, fieng, thun/that, todt, ward).

sentences.t: Es war ein armer Mann und eine arme Frau, die hatten nichts als eine kleine Hütte, und nährten sich vom Fischfang, und es gieng bei ihnen von Hand zu Mund.
sentences.l: There was a poor man and a poor woman; they had nothing but a little hut, and fed themselves from fishing, and with them it went from hand to mouth.
sentences.i: There was a poor man and a poor woman who had nothing but a little hut; they lived by fishing, and with them it was hand to mouth.
sentences.n: gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging (gehen). “sich nähren von” = to feed oneself on, to live by. “von Hand zu Mund” is the same image as the English hand to mouth: whatever is caught is eaten at once.

sentences.t: Es geschah aber, als der Mann eines Tages beim Wasser saß und sein Netz auswarf, daß er einen Fisch herauszog, der ganz golden war.
sentences.l: But it came to pass, as the man sat one day by the water and cast out his net, that he drew out a fish that was all golden.
sentences.i: But it came to pass one day, as the man sat by the water casting his net, that he drew out a fish that was all of gold.
sentences.n: “eines Tages” is a genitive of time — one day; German marks the time with a case rather than a preposition. auswerfen and herausziehen are both separable. “Es geschah aber, daß …” is this tale’s formula for the turn of events, and it comes again.

sentences.t: Und als er den Fisch voll Verwunderung betrachtete, hub dieser an zu reden und sprach „hör, Fischer, wirfst du mich wieder hinab ins Wasser, so mach ich deine kleine Hütte zu einem prächtigen Schloß.“
sentences.l: And as he regarded the fish full of wonder, this one began to speak and said “listen, fisherman, if you throw me down into the water again, then I make your little hut into a splendid castle.”
sentences.i: And as he looked at the fish in wonder, the fish began to speak, and said: “Listen, fisherman: if you throw me back down into the water, I will make your little hut into a splendid castle.”
sentences.n: hub is the old preterite of heben, here in anheben, to begin; modern German would say fing an. dieser, this one, points back to the fish and keeps the two apart. A conditional with no wenn: “wirfst du mich …” = if you throw me — the verb comes first and English must supply the “if”.

sentences.t: Da antwortete der Fischer „was hilft mir ein Schloß, wenn ich nichts zu essen habe?“
sentences.l: Then the fisherman answered “what does a castle help me, if I have nothing to eat?”
sentences.i: Then the fisherman answered: “What good is a castle to me if I have nothing to eat?”
sentences.n: helfen takes the dative, mir, and “was hilft mir …” is the fixed way of asking what use a thing is. “nichts zu essen haben” = to have nothing to eat, haben with zu and an infinitive.

sentences.t: Sprach der Goldfisch weiter „auch dafür soll gesorgt sein, es wird ein Schrank im Schloß sein, wenn du den aufschließest, so stehen Schüsseln darin mit den schönsten Speisen, so viel du dir wünschest.“
sentences.l: The goldfish spoke further “for that too shall be provided: there will be a cupboard in the castle, and if you unlock it, then dishes stand in it with the finest foods, as much as you wish for yourself.”
sentences.i: The goldfish went on: “That shall be seen to as well. There will be a cupboard in the castle, and when you unlock it, dishes will stand in it with the finest food, as much as you could wish for.”
sentences.n: The sentence opens with its verb — “Sprach der Goldfisch weiter” — a lively narrative inversion these tales are fond of, where English needs a subject first. “für etwas sorgen” = to see to a thing, here in the passive. den is a demonstrative standing for the cupboard, not an article.

sentences.t: „Wenn das ist,“ sprach der Mann, „so kann ich dir wohl den Gefallen thun.“
sentences.l: “If that is so,” spoke the man, “then I can well do you the favour.”
sentences.i: “If that is how it is,” said the man, “then I can do you the favour readily enough.”
sentences.n: thun is the 1857 spelling of tun. “einem einen Gefallen thun” = to do someone a favour, the person in the dative. The fisherman says du to the fish, as the fish says du to him.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sagte der Fisch, „es ist aber die Bedingung dabei, daß du keinem Menschen auf der Welt, wer es auch immer sein mag, entdeckst woher dein Glück gekommen ist;
sentences.l: “Yes,” said the fish, “but there is the condition with it, that you disclose to no one in the world, whoever it may ever be, from where your fortune has come;
sentences.i: “Yes,” said the fish, “but there is a condition attached: that you disclose to no living soul, whoever it may be, where your fortune came from;
sentences.n: entdecken here is not to discover but to disclose, to un-cover — the older sense. “wer es auch immer sein mag” = whoever it may be, a concessive with mögen. The verb entdeckst waits to the very end of its daß-clause, after a long insertion.

sentences.t: sprichst du ein einziges Wort, so ist alles vorbei.“
sentences.l: if you speak a single word, then everything is over.”
sentences.i: if you speak one single word, all is over.”
sentences.n: The wenn-less conditional again, verb first: “sprichst du …” = if you speak. This is the tale’s hinge, and it will be broken twice.

sentences.t: Nun warf der Mann den wunderbaren Fisch wieder ins Wasser und gieng heim.
sentences.l: Now the man threw the wonderful fish back into the water and went home.
sentences.n: wunderbar here keeps its full weight — full of wonder, miraculous — rather than the worn modern “wonderful”.

sentences.t: Wo aber sonst seine Hütte gestanden hatte, da stand jetzt ein großes Schloß.
sentences.l: But where his hut had formerly stood, there now stood a great castle.
sentences.i: Where his hut had stood before, a great castle now stood.
sentences.n: sonst here means formerly, at other times, not “otherwise”. The da that follows gathers up the wo-clause: where …, there.

sentences.t: Da machte er ein paar Augen, trat hinein und sah seine Frau, mit schönen Kleidern geputzt, in einer prächtigen Stube sitzen.
sentences.l: Then he made a pair of eyes, stepped in and saw his wife, decked out in fine clothes, sitting in a splendid room.
sentences.i: Then he opened his eyes wide, stepped in, and saw his wife sitting in a splendid room, decked out in fine clothes.
sentences.n: “ein paar Augen machen” = to stare, to open one’s eyes wide in astonishment. “sah … sitzen” — German uses the bare infinitive after a verb of perceiving where English uses the -ing form. Die Stube is the one heated living room of a house.

sentences.t: Sie war ganz vergnügt und sprach „Mann, wie ist das auf einmal gekommen? das gefällt mir wohl.“
sentences.l: She was quite delighted and spoke “husband, how has this come all at once? that pleases me well.”
sentences.i: She was in high delight, and said: “Husband, how has all this come about so suddenly? I like it well.”
sentences.n: Mann as a form of address means husband, not “man”. gefallen takes the dative: literally, that pleases to me. “auf einmal” = all at once, suddenly.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sagte der Mann, „es gefällt mir auch, aber es hungert mich auch gewaltig, gib mir erst was zu essen.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” said the man, “it pleases me too, but it also hungers me mightily — give me something to eat first.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said the man, “I like it too; but I am mightily hungry as well — give me something to eat first.”
sentences.n: “es hungert mich” is the old impersonal: it hungers me, with the person in the accusative; modern German says ich habe Hunger. was here is short for etwas.

sentences.t: Sprach die Frau „ich habe nichts und weiß in dem neuen Haus nichts zu finden.“
sentences.l: Spoke the wife “I have nothing and know nothing to find in the new house.”
sentences.i: The wife said: “I have nothing, and I know of nothing to be found in this new house.”
sentences.n: The verb-first opening again — Sprach die Frau. “nichts zu finden wissen” = not to know where to find anything, wissen with zu and an infinitive.

sentences.t: „Das hat keine Noth,“ sagte der Mann, „dort sehe ich einen großen Schrank, den schließ einmal auf.“
sentences.l: “That has no need,” said the man, “over there I see a great cupboard — just unlock that one.”
sentences.i: “That is no trouble,” said the man; “I see a great cupboard over there — just open it.”
sentences.n: “das hat keine Noth” = there is no difficulty in that, never mind that; Noth is the 1857 spelling of Not. den is again a demonstrative put first: that one. aufschließen is separable — schließ … auf.

sentences.t: Wie sie den Schrank aufschloß, stand da Kuchen, Fleisch, Obst, Wein, und lachte einen ordentlich an.
sentences.l: When she unlocked the cupboard, there stood cake, meat, fruit, wine, and fairly smiled upon one.
sentences.i: When she unlocked the cupboard, there stood cake, meat, fruit and wine, fairly smiling at you.
sentences.n: “einen anlachen” = to smile invitingly at one; einen is the accusative of the indefinite man, which English turns into “you”. ordentlich here means properly, thoroughly. One singular verb serves the whole list, as often in these tales.

sentences.t: Da rief die Frau voll Freude „Herz, was begehrst du nun?“ und sie setzten sich nieder, aßen und tranken zusammen.
sentences.l: Then the wife cried full of joy “heart, what do you desire now?” and they sat themselves down, ate and drank together.
sentences.i: Then the wife cried out in joy: “Heart, what more could you ask?” And they sat down, and ate and drank together.
sentences.n: A person addressing his or her own heart is a common turn in these tales. begehren = to desire, crave, a word of higher register than wollen. niedersetzen is separable.

sentences.t: Wie sie satt waren, fragte die Frau „aber, Mann, wo kommt all dieser Reichthum her?“
sentences.l: When they were full, the wife asked “but, husband, where does all this wealth come from?”
sentences.i: When they had eaten their fill, the wife asked: “But, husband, where does all this wealth come from?”
sentences.n: “wo … her” is a split pair, woher with its her thrown to the end — the mark of a question about origin. Reichthum is the 1857 spelling of Reichtum. wie at the head of the sentence means when, as.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ antwortete er, „frage mich nicht darum, ich darf dirs nicht sagen, wenn ichs jemand entdecke, so ist unser Glück wieder dahin.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” he answered, “do not ask me about it, I may not tell you — if I disclose it to anyone, then our fortune is gone again.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” he answered, “do not ask me about it. I dare not tell you. If I disclose it to anyone, our good fortune is gone again.”
sentences.n: dürfen is to be permitted, not to dare: I am not allowed to tell you. dirs = dir es, ichs = ich es. “dahin sein” = to be gone, done for.

sentences.t: „Gut,“ sprach sie, „wenn ichs nicht wissen soll, so begehr ichs auch nicht zu wissen.“
sentences.l: “Good,” she spoke, “if I am not to know it, then I do not desire to know it either.”
sentences.i: “Very well,” she said; “if I am not meant to know it, then I have no wish to know it.”
sentences.n: sollen here is what is laid on one from outside: if I am not meant to know. begehr stands for begehre, the -e dropped, as often in these tales.

sentences.t: Das war aber ihr Ernst nicht, es ließ ihr keine Ruhe Tag und Nacht,
sentences.l: But that was not her earnest; it left her no rest day and night,
sentences.i: But she did not mean it; it gave her no rest day or night,
sentences.n: “das ist mein Ernst” = I mean it in earnest; “ihr Ernst” is her true meaning. “es ließ ihr keine Ruhe” is impersonal — a nameless es is the subject, and the woman stands in the dative as the one it works on.

sentences.t: und sie quälte und stachelte den Mann so lang, bis er in der Ungeduld heraus sagte, es käme alles von einem wunderbaren goldenen Fisch, den er gefangen und dafür wieder in Freiheit gelassen hätte.
sentences.l: and she tormented and goaded the man so long, until in his impatience he said out that it all came from a wonderful golden fish which he had caught and had for that let go free again.
sentences.i: and she tormented and goaded the man so long that at last, out of all patience, he came out with it: that it all came from a wonderful golden fish which he had caught and set free again in return.
sentences.n: käme and hätte are the subjunctive of reported speech — the tale reports his words without quoting them, and English simply uses the past. “heraus sagen” = to come out with a thing; dafür = in return for that.

sentences.t: Und wies heraus war, da verschwand alsbald das schöne Schloß mit dem Schrank, und sie saßen wieder in der alten Fischerhütte.
sentences.l: And when it was out, at once the fine castle with the cupboard vanished, and they sat again in the old fisherman’s hut.
sentences.i: And once it was out, the fine castle vanished with its cupboard on the instant, and there they sat again in the old fisherman’s hut.
sentences.n: wies = wie es, and “heraus sein” = to be out, said aloud past recall. alsbald = at once, straightway.

sentences.t: Der Mann mußte von vornen anfangen seinem Gewerbe nachgehen und fischen.
sentences.l: The man had to begin from the front again, follow his trade and fish.
sentences.i: The man had to begin all over again, follow his trade and go fishing.
sentences.n: “von vornen anfangen” (modern von vorn) = to start again from the beginning. nachgehen takes the dative — seinem Gewerbe — and means to pursue, to attend to. The two infinitives simply follow anfangen with no zu, which is loose even for 1857.

sentences.t: Das Glück wollte es aber, daß er den goldenen Fisch noch einmal herauszog.
sentences.l: But luck would have it that he drew the golden fish out once more.
sentences.n: “das Glück wollte es, daß …” = luck would have it that. Glück is at once luck, fortune and happiness, and everything in this tale hangs on the word.

sentences.t: „Hör,“ sprach der Fisch, „wenn du mich wieder ins Wasser wirfst, so will ich dir noch einmal das Schloß mit dem Schrank voll Gesottenem und Gebratenem zurückgeben;
sentences.l: “Listen,” spoke the fish, “if you throw me into the water again, then I will give you back once more the castle with the cupboard full of boiled and roasted;
sentences.i: “Listen,” said the fish, “if you throw me back into the water, I will give you the castle again, with the cupboard full of boiled meat and roast;
sentences.n: Gesottenem and Gebratenem are participles used as nouns in the dative — boiled things and roasted things; the pair is the old standing phrase for a full table. zurückgeben is separable, its prefix at the end.

sentences.t: nur halt dich fest und verrath bei Leibe nicht von wem dus hast, sonst gehts wieder verloren.“
sentences.l: only hold yourself fast and do not for your life betray from whom you have it, or else it goes lost again.”
sentences.i: only hold fast, and on your life do not tell whom you have it from, or it will be lost again.”
sentences.n: “bei Leibe nicht” = on no account — an old oath-formula, by one’s body. verrath is the 1857 spelling of verrat (verraten). “verloren gehen” = to be lost, to go astray; dus = du es, gehts = geht es.

sentences.t: „Ich will mich schon hüten“ antwortete der Fischer und warf den Fisch in sein Wasser hinab.
sentences.l: “I shall take good care,” answered the fisherman, and threw the fish down into his water.
sentences.n: “sich hüten” = to be on one’s guard, to take care not to do a thing; schon is the little word of assurance: never fear. The 1857 text prints no comma before antwortete, and the punctuation stands as printed.

sentences.t: Daheim war nun alles wieder in voriger Herrlichkeit, und die Frau war in einer Freude über das Glück;
sentences.l: At home everything was now again in former splendour, and the wife was in a joy over the good fortune;
sentences.i: At home everything was in its former splendour again, and the wife was in raptures over their good fortune;
sentences.n: “in einer Freude sein” — the indefinite article before an abstract noun gives it force: in such a joy. vorig = former, previous.

sentences.t: aber die Neugierde ließ ihr doch keine Ruhe, daß sie nach ein paar Tagen wieder zu fragen anhub wie es zugegangen wäre und wie er es angefangen habe.
sentences.l: but curiosity left her no rest, so that after a couple of days she began to ask again how it had come about and how he had set about it.
sentences.i: but curiosity gave her no rest, so that after a few days she began asking again how it had come about and how he had managed it.
sentences.n: anhub is the old preterite of anheben, to begin — separable, its an waiting to the end. wäre and habe are both the subjunctive of a reported question, and the tale slips from the one form to the other without any change of sense. “zugehen” = to come about, to happen.

sentences.t: Der Mann schwieg eine Zeitlang still dazu, endlich aber machte sie ihn so ärgerlich, daß er herausplatzte und das Geheimnis verrieth.
sentences.l: The man kept silent to it for a time, but at last she made him so annoyed that he burst out and betrayed the secret.
sentences.i: The man kept silent about it for a while; but at last she made him so angry that he burst out with it and betrayed the secret.
sentences.n: “still schweigen” doubles the idea — to be silent quietly — for emphasis. herausplatzen = to burst out with a thing, separable. verrieth is the 1857 spelling of verriet. Note that the 1857 text prints Geheimnis with plain s where it writes daß and muß with ß; the spelling stands as printed.

sentences.t: In dem Augenblick verschwand das Schloß und sie saßen wieder in der alten Hütte.
sentences.l: In that instant the castle vanished and they sat again in the old hut.

sentences.t: „Nun hast dus,“ sagte der Mann, „jetzt können wir wieder am Hungertuch nagen.“
sentences.l: “Now you have it,” said the man, “now we can gnaw at the hunger-cloth again.”
sentences.i: “Now you have what you wanted,” said the man; “now we can go back to gnawing the hunger-cloth.”
sentences.n: “am Hungertuch nagen” = to be starving, to live in the barest poverty. The Hungertuch was the cloth hung before the altar in Lent, when the church stood bare and the fast was kept; to gnaw it is proverbial destitution. dus = du es.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sprach die Frau, „ich will den Reichthum lieber nicht, wenn ich nicht weiß von wem er kommt; sonst habe ich doch keine Ruhe.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” spoke the wife, “I would rather not have the wealth, if I do not know from whom it comes; otherwise I have no rest at all.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” said the wife, “I would rather not have the wealth if I am not to know where it comes from; otherwise I get no peace.”
sentences.n: “lieber nicht wollen” = to prefer not to; lieber is the comparative of gern. doch presses the point: no rest at all, you see.

sentences.t: Der Mann gieng wieder fischen, und über eine Zeit so wars nicht anders, er holte den Goldfisch zum drittenmal heraus.
sentences.l: The man went fishing again, and after a time it was no different: he drew the goldfish out for the third time.
sentences.i: The man went fishing again, and after a while it was no different — he pulled out the goldfish for the third time.
sentences.n: “über eine Zeit” = after a time. The so that follows it is resumptive, gathering up the phrase before it; German often marks its main clause this way and English leaves it out. wars = war es. Three times over is the backbone of the tale.

sentences.t: „Hör,“ sprach der Fisch: „ich sehe wohl, ich soll immer wieder in deine Hände fallen,
sentences.l: “Listen,” spoke the fish, “I see well, I am always to fall into your hands again,
sentences.i: “Listen,” said the fish, “I see how it is — I am fated to fall into your hands again and again;
sentences.n: sollen here is what fate lays down: I am destined to. wohl strengthens the verb of perceiving: I see clearly enough.

sentences.t: nimm mich mit nach Haus, und zerschneid mich in sechs Stücke, zwei davon gieb deiner Frau zu essen, zwei deinem Pferd, und zwei leg in die Erde, so wirst du Segen davon haben.“
sentences.l: take me with you home, and cut me into six pieces; two of them give your wife to eat, two your horse, and two lay in the earth, then you will have blessing from it.”
sentences.i: take me home with you and cut me into six pieces; two of them give your wife to eat, two to your horse, and two lay in the earth; then you will have a blessing from it.”
sentences.n: gieb is the 1857 spelling of gib (geben); it, zerschneid, nimm and leg are all imperatives without the -e. mitnehmen is separable — nimm … mit. Segen is blessing in the concrete sense of increase and fruitfulness, as the next sentence shows.

sentences.t: Der Mann nahm den Fisch mit nach Haus und that wie er ihm gesagt hatte.
sentences.l: The man took the fish home with him and did as it had told him.
sentences.i: The man took the fish home with him and did as the fish had told him.
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat (thun, modern tun). ihm could be either the fish or the man; German leaves the little pronoun to be sorted out by the sense.

sentences.t: Es geschah aber, daß aus den zwei Stücken, die in die Erde gelegt waren, zwei goldene Lilien aufwuchsen, und daß das Pferd zwei goldene Füllen bekam, und des Fischers Frau zwei Kinder gebar, die ganz golden waren.
sentences.l: But it came to pass that out of the two pieces that were laid in the earth two golden lilies grew up, and that the horse got two golden foals, and the fisherman’s wife bore two children who were all golden.
sentences.i: But it came to pass that from the two pieces laid in the earth two golden lilies grew up, that the horse bore two golden foals, and that the fisherman’s wife bore two children who were all of gold.
sentences.n: “des Fischers Frau” is the old genitive standing before its noun, where modern German says die Frau des Fischers. aufwachsen is separable. The three parallel daß-clauses hold the three births in a single breath.

sentences.t: Die Kinder wuchsen heran, wurden groß und schön, und die Lilien und Pferde wuchsen mit ihnen.
sentences.l: The children grew up, grew big and fair, and the lilies and horses grew with them.
sentences.i: The children grew up, grew tall and fair, and the lilies and the horses grew along with them.

sentences.t: Da sprachen sie „Vater, wir wollen uns auf unsere goldenen Rosse setzen und in die Welt ausziehen.“
sentences.l: Then they spoke “father, we will seat ourselves on our golden steeds and set out into the world.”
sentences.i: Then they said: “Father, we mean to mount our golden steeds and go out into the world.”
sentences.n: Roß is the higher word for a horse — steed — beside the ordinary Pferd of the line before. “in die Welt ausziehen” = to set out into the world, the standard opening of a tale’s journey; ausziehen is separable.

sentences.t: Er aber antwortete betrübt „wie will ichs aushalten, wenn ihr fortzieht und ich nicht weiß wies euch geht?“
sentences.l: But he answered sorrowfully “how will I bear it, if you go away and I do not know how it goes with you?”
sentences.i: But he answered sadly: “How am I to bear it, if you go away and I do not know how you fare?”
sentences.n: “es geht mir gut” = I am doing well, the fixed impersonal with the person in the dative; wies = wie es. aushalten and fortziehen are both separable. wollen here comes close to the English future: how shall I bear it.

sentences.t: Da sagten sie „die zwei goldenen Lilien bleiben hier, daran könnt ihr sehen, wies uns geht:
sentences.l: Then they said “the two golden lilies stay here; by them you can see how it goes with us:
sentences.i: Then they said: “The two golden lilies stay here; by them you can see how we fare:
sentences.n: daran = by that, an folded together with the pronoun. The sons address their father as ihr, the older respectful plural used to parents.

sentences.t: sind sie frisch, so sind wir gesund; sind sie welk, so sind wir krank; fallen sie um, so sind wir todt.“
sentences.l: if they are fresh, then we are healthy; if they are withered, then we are sick; if they fall over, then we are dead.”
sentences.i: if they are fresh, we are well; if they wilt, we are sick; if they fall over, we are dead.”
sentences.n: Three conditionals without wenn, each with its verb first and each answered by so — the pattern at its clearest. todt is the 1857 spelling of tot.

sentences.t: Sie ritten fort und kamen in ein Wirthshaus, darin waren viele Leute, und als sie die zwei Goldkinder erblickten, fiengen sie an zu lachen und zu spotten.
sentences.l: They rode away and came into an inn; in it were many people, and when they caught sight of the two gold-children, they began to laugh and to mock.
sentences.i: They rode away and came to an inn where there were many people; and when these caught sight of the two gold-children, they began to laugh and jeer.
sentences.n: fiengen is the 1857 spelling of fingen (anfangen), separable. Wirthshaus is the 1857 Wirtshaus. The second sie is the people, not the brothers — German lets the one pronoun serve both and leaves the sense to sort it out.

sentences.t: Wie der eine das Gespött hörte, so schämte er sich, wollte nicht in die Welt, kehrte um und kam wieder heim zu seinem Vater.
sentences.l: When the one heard the mockery, he was ashamed, would not [go] into the world, turned about and came home again to his father.
sentences.i: When the one of them heard the mockery he was ashamed, would have no more of the world, turned about and came home again to his father.
sentences.n: “sich schämen” = to be ashamed, reflexive. “wollte nicht in die Welt” drops the verb of motion after the modal once more, and the literal supplies [go]. umkehren is separable.

sentences.t: Der andere aber ritt fort und gelangte zu einem großen Wald.
sentences.l: But the other rode on and came to a great forest.

sentences.t: Und als er hinein reiten wollte, sprachen die Leute „es geht nicht, daß ihr durchreitet,
sentences.l: And when he wanted to ride in, the people spoke “it will not do that you ride through,
sentences.i: And when he was for riding in, the people said: “It will not do for you to ride through;
sentences.n: “es geht nicht” = it will not do, it cannot be done. hinein marks motion inward away from the speaker; German has a whole set of such words — hinein, heraus, hinab — that English folds into in, out, down.

sentences.t: der Wald ist voll Räuber, die werden übel mit euch umgehen, und gar, wenn sie sehen daß ihr golden seid und euere Pferde auch, so werden sie euch todt schlagen.“
sentences.l: the forest is full of robbers; they will deal ill with you, and above all, if they see that you are golden and your horses too, then they will strike you dead.”
sentences.i: the forest is full of robbers, and they will handle you badly; and above all, if they see that you are golden and your horses too, they will strike you dead.”
sentences.n: “mit jemandem umgehen” = to deal with, to treat someone. gar here is an intensifier: worse still, above all. euere is an older spelling of eure. todt schlagen stands apart where modern German writes totschlagen.

sentences.t: Er aber ließ sich nicht schrecken und sprach „ich muß und soll hindurch.“
sentences.l: But he did not let himself be frightened and spoke “I must and shall through.”
sentences.i: But he would not be frightened, and said: “I must and will get through.”
sentences.n: “sich nicht schrecken lassen” = not to let oneself be scared off. “ich muß und soll” pairs the two modals for sheer insistence — must, and am bound to; the verb of motion is left out again, and the phrase will come back twice more.

sentences.t: Da nahm er Bärenfelle und überzog sich und sein Pferd damit, daß nichts mehr vom Gold zu sehen war, und ritt getrost in den Wald hinein.
sentences.l: Then he took bear-skins and drew them over himself and his horse, so that nothing more of the gold was to be seen, and rode confidently into the forest.
sentences.i: Then he took bear-skins and covered himself and his horse with them, so that nothing of the gold could be seen any more, and rode boldly into the forest.
sentences.n: “zu sehen war” — sein with zu and an infinitive is a passive of possibility: was to be seen, could be seen. daß here means so that. getrost = confident, of good courage.

sentences.t: Als er ein wenig fortgeritten war, so hörte er es in den Gebüschen rauschen und vernahm Stimmen, die miteinander sprachen.
sentences.l: When he had ridden on a little, he heard it rustling in the bushes and made out voices that spoke with one another.
sentences.i: When he had ridden on a little, he heard a rustling in the bushes and made out voices talking together.
sentences.n: “hörte er es … rauschen” — the bare infinitive after a verb of perceiving, with an empty es for whatever rustles. vernehmen = to perceive, to catch by ear, higher in register than hören.

sentences.t: Von der einen Seite riefs „da ist einer,“ von der andern aber „laß ihn laufen, das ist ein Bärenhäuter, und arm und kahl, wie eine Kirchenmaus, was sollen wir mit ihm anfangen!“
sentences.l: From the one side it called “there is one,” but from the other “let him go — that is a bear-skin wearer, and poor and bare as a church mouse; what are we to begin with him!”
sentences.i: From one side a voice called: “There is one!” — but from the other: “Let him go; that is a bearskin fellow, poor and bare as a church mouse. What should we want with him!”
sentences.n: riefs = rief es, with a nameless es for the unseen speaker. Ein Bärenhäuter, a wearer of bear-skins, was a byword for a ragged idler — a word of contempt, and the tale plays on it, since he is wearing bear-skins in fact. “arm wie eine Kirchenmaus” is the same proverb as poor as a church mouse. “was sollen wir mit ihm anfangen” = what are we to do with him.

sentences.t: So ritt das Goldkind glücklich durch den Wald und geschah ihm kein Leid.
sentences.l: So the gold-child rode happily through the forest, and no harm happened to him.
sentences.i: So the gold-child rode safely through the forest, and no harm came to him.
sentences.n: glücklich here means safely, with good fortune, rather than in good spirits — the same doubleness as in Glück. “jemandem geschieht ein Leid” = harm befalls someone, the person in the dative; the second clause repeats no subject, and English has to supply one.

sentences.t: Eines Tags kam er in ein Dorf, darin sah er ein Mädchen, das war so schön, daß er nicht glaubte es könnte ein schöneres auf der Welt sein.
sentences.l: One day he came into a village; in it he saw a girl, and she was so fair that he did not believe there could be a fairer one in the world.
sentences.i: One day he came to a village, and there he saw a girl so fair that he did not believe there could be a fairer in the world.
sentences.n: “eines Tags” is a genitive of time, a shorter form of eines Tages. könnte is the subjunctive of reported thought, where English says “could”. Mädchen is neuter because of its diminutive ending, so the tale calls the girl das and es — a thing English cannot copy.

sentences.t: Und weil er eine so große Liebe zu ihm empfand, so gieng er zu ihm und sagte „ich habe dich von ganzem Herzen lieb, willst du meine Frau werden?“
sentences.l: And because he felt so great a love toward it, he went to it and said “I have you dear from my whole heart — will you become my wife?”
sentences.i: And because he felt so great a love for her, he went to her and said: “I love you with all my heart; will you be my wife?”
sentences.n: The two ihm are neuter pronouns for das Mädchen, so the German says “it” where English must say “her”. “jemanden lieb haben” = to love someone, with lieb standing apart from the verb.

sentences.t: Er gefiel aber auch dem Mädchen so sehr, daß es einwilligte und sprach „ja, ich will deine Frau werden und dir treu sein mein Lebelang.“
sentences.l: But he pleased the girl so much too that it consented and spoke “yes, I will become your wife and be true to you my life long.”
sentences.i: But he pleased the girl so well too that she consented, and said: “Yes, I will be your wife and true to you my whole life long.”
sentences.n: gefallen with the dative once more: he was pleasing to the girl. “mein Lebelang” is an accusative of duration with no preposition — for my whole life; modern German writes mein Leben lang.

sentences.t: Nun hielten sie Hochzeit zusammen, und als sie eben in der größten Freude waren, kam der Vater der Braut heim,
sentences.l: Now they held wedding together, and just as they were in the greatest joy, the bride’s father came home,
sentences.i: So they held their wedding together; and just as the joy was at its height, the bride’s father came home,
sentences.n: “Hochzeit halten” = to hold a wedding, the fixed phrase, with no article. eben here means just, at that very moment. heimkommen is separable.

sentences.t: und als er sah daß seine Tochter Hochzeit machte, verwunderte er sich und sprach „wo ist der Bräutigam?“
sentences.l: and when he saw that his daughter was making a wedding, he wondered and spoke “where is the bridegroom?”
sentences.i: and when he saw that his daughter was being married, he was astonished, and said: “Where is the bridegroom?”
sentences.n: “sich verwundern” = to be astonished, reflexive. The 1857 text prints no comma before the daß-clause, and the punctuation stands as printed.

sentences.t: Sie zeigten ihm das Goldkind, das hatte aber noch seine Bärenfelle um.
sentences.l: They showed him the gold-child, but that one still had its bear-skins on.
sentences.i: They showed him the gold-child; but he still had his bear-skins on.
sentences.n: “um haben” = to have something on, wrapped about one — separable, the um standing at the end with no verb of its own. das is a demonstrative gathering up the noun before it: that one.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Vater zornig „nimmermehr soll ein Bärenhäuter meine Tochter haben,“ und wollte ihn ermorden.
sentences.l: Then the father spoke angrily “nevermore shall a bear-skin wearer have my daughter,” and wanted to murder him.
sentences.i: Then the father said angrily: “Never shall a bearskin fellow have my daughter” — and he made to murder him.
sentences.n: sollen in a decree is shall: never shall he have her. wollte here is on the point of, made to, rather than merely wished — and the tale does not soften what the father intends.

sentences.t: Da bat ihn die Braut, was sie konnte, und sprach „er ist einmal mein Mann, und ich habe ihn von Herzen lieb,“ bis er sich endlich besänftigen ließ.
sentences.l: Then the bride begged him what she could, and spoke “he is once for all my husband, and I have him dear from my heart,” until he at last let himself be appeased.
sentences.i: Then the bride begged him all she could, and said: “He is my husband now, and I love him with all my heart” — until at last he let himself be appeased.
sentences.n: “was sie konnte” = as much as she could. einmal is the little word of settled fact: he is my husband, and there is an end of it. “sich besänftigen lassen” = to let oneself be soothed.

sentences.t: Doch aber kams ihm nicht aus den Gedanken, so daß er am andern Morgen früh aufstand und seiner Tochter Mann sehen wollte, ob er ein gemeiner und verlumpter Bettler wäre.
sentences.l: Yet all the same it did not come out of his thoughts, so that the next morning he got up early and wanted to see his daughter’s husband, whether he were a common and ragged beggar.
sentences.i: Yet for all that it would not go out of his mind, so that next morning he rose early to see his daughter’s husband, and whether he were a common ragged beggar.
sentences.n: “doch aber” doubles the concession — yet nevertheless. kams = kam es. “seiner Tochter Mann” is again the old genitive placed before its noun. wäre is the subjunctive of an indirect question.

sentences.t: Wie er aber hinblickte, sah er einen herrlichen, goldenen Mann im Bette, und die abgeworfenen Bärenfelle lagen auf der Erde.
sentences.l: But when he looked over, he saw a glorious golden man in the bed, and the thrown-off bear-skins lay on the ground.
sentences.i: But when he looked, he saw a glorious golden man in the bed, and the cast-off bear-skins lying on the floor.
sentences.n: hinblicken = to look over toward a thing, separable. “die abgeworfenen Bärenfelle” is an attributive participle standing before its noun — the thrown-off skins — which English can copy here. Bette carries the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Da gieng er zurück und dachte „wie gut ists, daß ich meinen Zorn bändigte, ich hätte eine große Missethat begangen.“
sentences.l: Then he went back and thought “how good it is that I curbed my anger — I would have committed a great misdeed.”
sentences.i: Then he went back, and thought: “How good it is that I curbed my anger; I should have done a great wrong.”
sentences.n: Missethat is the 1857 spelling of Missetat, a misdeed. hätte … begangen is the past subjunctive of the unreal: I would have committed. ists = ist es.

sentences.t: Dem Goldkind aber träumte er zöge hinaus auf die Jagd nach einem prächtigen Hirsch, und als er am Morgen erwachte, sprach er zu seiner Braut „ich will hinaus auf die Jagd.“
sentences.l: But to the gold-child it dreamt that he was riding out to the hunt after a splendid stag; and when he awoke in the morning, he spoke to his bride “I will out to the hunt.”
sentences.i: But the gold-child dreamt that he rode out hunting after a splendid stag; and when he awoke in the morning he said to his bride: “I mean to go out hunting.”
sentences.n: “mir träumt” is the old impersonal: it dreams to me, with the dreamer in the dative — Dem Goldkind. zöge is the subjunctive of the dream’s content, reported rather than asserted. Once again a modal stands without its verb of motion, and English supplies “go”.

sentences.t: Ihr war angst, und sie bat ihn da zu bleiben und sagte „leicht kann dir ein großes Unglück begegnen,“ aber er antwortete „ich soll und muß fort.“
sentences.l: To her it was anxious, and she begged him to stay there and said “easily can a great misfortune meet you,” but he answered “I shall and must away.”
sentences.i: She was frightened, and begged him to stay, and said: “A great misfortune may easily meet you”; but he answered: “I shall and must go.”
sentences.n: “mir ist angst” = I am afraid, again with the person in the dative and no subject at all. leicht here means easily, all too readily. begegnen takes the dative, dir. “ich soll und muß fort” is the same formula he used before riding into the forest.

sentences.t: Da stand er auf und zog hinaus in den Wald, und gar nicht lange, so hielt auch ein stolzer Hirsch vor ihm, ganz nach seinem Traume.
sentences.l: Then he got up and went out into the forest, and not long at all, and there stood a proud stag before him, quite according to his dream.
sentences.i: Then he got up and went out into the forest; and it was no long while before a proud stag stood before him, exactly as in his dream.
sentences.n: “und gar nicht lange, so …” leaves out the verb altogether — not long, and then; German can carry the clause on the so alone. stolz of a beast is proud in the sense of splendid, high-bearing. aufstehen and hinausziehen are separable.

sentences.t: Er legte an und wollte ihn schießen, aber der Hirsch sprang fort.
sentences.l: He laid [his gun] on and wanted to shoot it, but the stag sprang away.
sentences.i: He took aim and was about to shoot it, but the stag bounded away.
sentences.n: anlegen of a gun = to level it, to take aim — separable, legte … an; the German names no weapon, so the literal supplies [his gun]. wollte again marks the act on the point of being done.

sentences.t: Da jagte er ihm nach, über Graben und durch Gebüsche, und ward nicht müde den ganzen Tag; am Abend aber verschwand der Hirsch vor seinen Augen.
sentences.l: Then he chased after it, over ditch and through bushes, and did not grow tired the whole day; but in the evening the stag vanished before his eyes.
sentences.i: Then he gave chase, over ditch and through bushes, and did not tire the whole day long; but in the evening the stag vanished before his eyes.
sentences.n: nachjagen is separable and takes the dative — ihm, after it. ward is the old preterite of werden, modern wurde. “den ganzen Tag” is an accusative of duration with no preposition.

sentences.t: Und als das Goldkind sich umsah, so stand er vor einem kleinen Haus, darin saß eine Hexe.
sentences.l: And when the gold-child looked about him, he stood before a little house; in it sat a witch.
sentences.i: And when the gold-child looked about him, he was standing before a little house, and in it sat a witch.
sentences.n: Goldkind is neuter, but the tale drops straight back into er for him — grammar and sense pull opposite ways, and the sense wins. “sich umsehen” = to look about one, separable; darin = in it.

sentences.t: Er klopfte an, und ein Mütterchen kam heraus und fragte „was wollt ihr so spät noch mitten in dem großen Wald?“
sentences.l: He knocked, and a little mother came out and asked “what do you want still so late in the middle of the great forest?”
sentences.i: He knocked, and a little old woman came out and asked: “What do you want here so late, in the middle of the great forest?”
sentences.n: anklopfen is separable. Mütterchen, little mother, is the ordinary kindly word for an old woman — and the tale has just told us she is a witch. wollen with no infinitive means simply to want a thing.

sentences.t: Er sprach „habt ihr keinen Hirsch gesehen?“
sentences.l: He spoke “have you seen no stag?”
sentences.i: He said: “Have you seen a stag?”
sentences.n: German negates the noun — keinen Hirsch, no stag — where English negates the verb and says “not … a”.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ antwortete sie, „den Hirsch kenn ich wohl,“ und ein Hündlein, das mit ihr aus dem Haus gekommen war, bellte dabei den Mann heftig an.
sentences.l: “Yes,” she answered, “that stag I know well,” and a little dog that had come out of the house with her barked violently at the man the while.
sentences.i: “Yes,” she answered, “I know that stag well” — and a little dog that had come out of the house with her barked furiously at the man all the while.
sentences.n: den Hirsch is thrown to the front for emphasis, which pushes the verb into second place: that stag, I know him. kenn stands for kenne, the -e dropped as in speech. anbellen is separable — bellte … an. Her knowing the stag so well is the first sign that the stag was her doing.

sentences.t: „Willst du schweigen, du böse Kröte,“ sprach er, „sonst schieß ich dich todt.“
sentences.l: “Will you be silent, you wicked toad,” he spoke, “or else I shoot you dead.”
sentences.i: “Will you be quiet, you wicked toad,” he said, “or I shall shoot you dead.”
sentences.n: “willst du schweigen” is a command in the shape of a question, as English has it too. Kröte, toad, is abuse aimed at the dog. todt is the 1857 spelling of tot, and todtschießen is separable.

sentences.t: Da rief die Hexe zornig „was, mein Hündchen willst du tödten!“ und verwandelte ihn alsbald, daß er da lag wie ein Stein,
sentences.l: Then the witch cried angrily “what, you want to kill my little dog!” and transformed him at once, so that he lay there like a stone,
sentences.i: Then the witch cried out angrily: “What, you would kill my little dog!” — and on the instant she transformed him, so that he lay there like a stone;
sentences.n: “mein Hündchen” is thrown to the front before the modal, out of indignation. tödten is the 1857 spelling of töten. At the moment of the change the German says only that he lay there like a stone, without naming what he became; the next paragraph calls him Stein outright, and the apparatus keeps that order and adds nothing.

sentences.t: und seine Braut erwartete ihn umsonst und dachte „es ist gewiß eingetroffen, was mir so Angst machte und so schwer auf dem Herzen lag.“
sentences.l: and his bride waited for him in vain and thought “it has surely come true, what made me so afraid and lay so heavy on my heart.”
sentences.i: and his bride waited for him in vain, and thought: “Surely the very thing has come to pass that made me so afraid and lay so heavy on my heart.”
sentences.n: umsonst = in vain (it also means free of charge). eintreffen = to come true, to be fulfilled, separable. “einem Angst machen” = to frighten someone, the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Daheim aber stand der andere Bruder bei den Goldlilien, als plötzlich eine davon umfiel.
sentences.l: But at home the other brother stood by the golden lilies, when suddenly one of them fell over.
sentences.i: But at home the other brother was standing by the golden lilies when suddenly one of them fell over.

sentences.t: „Ach Gott,“ sprach er, „meinem Bruder ist ein großes Unglück zugestoßen, ich muß fort, ob ich ihn vielleicht errette.“
sentences.l: “Ah God,” he spoke, “a great misfortune has befallen my brother, I must away, whether I may perhaps save him.”
sentences.i: “Ah God,” he said, “a great misfortune has befallen my brother. I must be off, and see whether I can save him.”
sentences.n: zustoßen = to befall, with the person in the dative — meinem Bruder. ob here does not open a question but the purpose of the attempt: to see if. “ich muß fort” drops the verb of motion after the modal once more.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Vater „bleib hier, wenn ich auch dich verliere, was soll ich anfangen?“
sentences.l: Then the father said “stay here; if I lose you too, what shall I begin?”
sentences.i: Then the father said: “Stay here. If I lose you as well, what am I to do?”
sentences.n: “was soll ich anfangen” = what am I to do, what is to become of me; anfangen here is not to begin but to set about, to manage. bleib is the imperative without its -e.

sentences.t: Er aber antwortete „ich soll und muß fort.“
sentences.l: But he answered “I shall and must away.”

sentences.t: Da setzte er sich auf sein goldenes Pferd und ritt fort und kam in den großen Wald, wo sein Bruder lag und Stein war.
sentences.l: Then he set himself on his golden horse and rode away and came into the great forest, where his brother lay and was stone.
sentences.i: Then he mounted his golden horse and rode away, and came into the great forest where his brother lay and was stone.
sentences.n: “Stein war” without an article — he was stone, the substance itself, not a stone. The three ands in a row are the tale’s plain style, and are better kept than tidied away.

sentences.t: Die alte Hexe kam aus ihrem Haus, rief ihn an und wollte ihn auch berücken, aber er näherte sich nicht, sondern sprach „ich schieße dich nieder, wenn du meinen Bruder nicht wieder lebendig machst.“
sentences.l: The old witch came out of her house, called to him and wanted to beguile him too, but he did not come near, but spoke “I shoot you down, if you do not make my brother alive again.”
sentences.i: The old witch came out of her house, called to him, and would have beguiled him too; but he did not come near, and said: “I will shoot you down if you do not make my brother alive again.”
sentences.n: berücken = to beguile, to catch by a spell — an old word, faintly alive still in berückend, enchanting. anrufen and niederschießen are separable. sondern is the “but” that must follow a negative.

sentences.t: Sie rührte, so ungerne sies auch that, den Stein mit dem Finger an, und alsbald erhielt er sein menschliches Leben zurück.
sentences.l: She touched the stone with her finger, unwillingly as she did it, and at once he received his human life back.
sentences.i: She touched the stone with her finger, little as she liked doing it, and at once he had his human life back again.
sentences.n: anrühren is separable, and here the whole concessive clause stands between the verb and its prefix — rührte … an. “so ungerne … auch” = however unwillingly. sies = sie es, and that is the 1857 spelling of tat.

sentences.t: Die beiden Goldkinder aber freuten sich, als sie sich wiedersahen, küßten und herzten sich, und ritten zusammen fort aus dem Wald, der eine zu seiner Braut, der andere heim zu seinem Vater.
sentences.l: But the two gold-children rejoiced when they saw each other again, kissed and embraced one another, and rode away together out of the forest, the one to his bride, the other home to his father.
sentences.i: But the two gold-children rejoiced when they saw each other again; they kissed and embraced, and rode away together out of the forest, the one to his bride, the other home to his father.
sentences.n: herzen = to press to one’s heart, to embrace; the pair küßten und herzten is a fixed one. “sich wiedersehen” = to see one another again.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Vater „ich wußte wohl, daß du deinen Bruder erlöst hattest, denn die goldene Lilie ist auf einmal wieder aufgestanden und hat fortgeblüht.“
sentences.l: Then the father spoke “I knew well that you had delivered your brother, for the golden lily has all at once stood up again and has gone on blooming.”
sentences.i: Then the father said: “I knew well that you had freed your brother, for all at once the golden lily stood up again and went on blooming.”
sentences.n: erlösen = to release, to redeem — the standard word in these tales for breaking an enchantment. aufstehen and fortblühen are separable, and the German perfect stands where English uses the simple past.

sentences.t: Nun lebten sie vergnügt, und es gieng ihnen wohl bis an ihr Ende.
sentences.l: Now they lived contented, and it went well with them until their end.
sentences.i: And now they lived in contentment, and all went well with them to the end of their days.
sentences.n: “es geht ihnen wohl” is the same impersonal with the dative that opened the tale, where it went from hand to mouth with them. This is the closing formula: not happily ever after, but simply, it went well with them to the end.
